metaDescription: Six corded and cordless electric chainsaws compared on bar length, motor, battery platform and safety features for limbing, firewood and storm cleanup.
expertTake: The EGO 56V 16 inch is the best overall pick because its brushless motor and large battery platform deliver gas-class cuts without fuel. The Oregon CS1500 corded saw is the value pick for owners who always work near an outlet. Anyone felling large trees or cutting several cords of firewood each year should skip electric and buy a gas saw.
introParagraphs: An electric chainsaw replaces the gas engine with a motor that runs from a cord or a battery. It starts with a switch, makes far less noise and needs no fuel mixing, which suits homeowners who cut a few times a year and hate small-engine upkeep.

The split that matters is corded versus cordless, then bar length and battery size. Cords give unlimited runtime but tether you to an outlet, while battery saws trade runtime for freedom. This guide ranks six saws and explains where electric stops being enough.

products.name: EGO Power+ 16-Inch 56V Cordless Chainsaw 2.5Ah Kit
products.description:
The EGO 16 inch pairs a brushless motor with a 56V battery from a platform that covers mowers, trimmers and blowers. The maker rates the 2.5Ah pack at up to 130 cuts through a 4 by 4, which gives a sense of how far one charge goes. A 16 inch bar is long enough for most storm limbs and small firewood rounds.

The tradeoff is that the 2.5Ah kit is the entry pack. Heavy firewood sessions will drain it, and a larger pack costs extra. Against the EGO 4.0Ah kit with the same 16 inch bar, this one gives up capacity but saves cost, and next to the Greenworks 40V it offers a higher voltage and a broader platform.

Ownership is easy because EGO supports its platform long term. Fill the bar oil, check chain tension before use, sharpen when cuts turn powdery and store the battery indoors in winter.
products.bestFor: Owners already on the EGO platform who want a capable 16 inch saw.
pros: 16 inch bar suits most homeowner jobs

products.name: Greenworks 40V 16-Inch Cordless Chainsaw Kit 4Ah
products.description:
The Greenworks 16 inch combines a 1.5kW brushless motor with a 4Ah battery, which is a bigger pack than the EGO 2.5Ah kit. A 16 inch bar handles limbing, small felling and firewood bucking. The brushless motor runs cooler and avoids brush wear.

The tradeoff is platform depth and refinement. The 40V line is smaller than EGO's 56V line, and the saw is a generic homeowner design. Against the Greenworks 12 inch kit in the lightweight guide, it adds bar length and a bigger battery but also weight.

Upkeep is standard: oil the bar, keep the chain sharp and tension correct, and store the pack indoors. Check the oiler line occasionally for clogs, because sawdust and thickened winter oil can starve the bar without any warning sound, and wipe the battery contacts so that dust does not cause intermittent cutouts under load.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who want a 16 inch cordless saw with a larger pack in the box.
cons: Pack is still limited for all-day cutting

products.name: SEESII 40V 16-Inch Brushless Cordless Chainsaw 2 x 4Ah
products.description:
The SEESII 16 inch ships with two 4Ah batteries, so one can charge while the other cuts. A brushless motor with a claimed 2000W rating gives the headline power, though wattage claims on newer brands are not directly comparable to established makers.

The tradeoff is brand support and platform. Batteries are proprietary, parts supply depends on one seller and there is no wider tool range. Against the Greenworks 40V it offers a second battery in the box, which is the practical advantage for a long job.

Expect to keep a close eye on the chain tension and oil level. Charge both packs before a session and rotate them. Because the platform is standalone, plan on buying a spare pack from the same seller while it is still listed, since a saw whose battery goes out of production becomes dead weight. Treat the 2000W figure as marketing and judge the saw by how it behaves on a seasoned oak limb rather than by the number on the box.
products.bestFor: Occasional users who want two batteries in the box.

products.name: SENIX 18-Inch 15-Amp Corded Electric Chainsaw CSE15-M
products.description:
The SENIX is an 18 inch corded saw with a 15 amp motor, which is the longest bar in this guide. A cord means unlimited runtime, so firewood bucking sessions are not interrupted by a depleted pack.

The tradeoff is the tether and the weight. You need an extension cord that is heavy enough for the amperage, and the cord is a trip hazard. Against the CRAFTSMAN 16 inch corded saw it gives a bar two inches longer, but it weighs more.

Keep the cord short and the right gauge, oil the bar before each use and keep the chain tight and sharp. Unplug before any adjustment. Drape the cord over your shoulder or route it behind you so the saw never crosses it, and coil it neatly after use because a kinked cord develops hidden damage that shows up as a hot plug and sluggish performance a few seasons later.
products.bestFor: Yard work close to an outlet where a long bar and unlimited run matter.
pros: 18 inch bar is the longest here
cons: Cord is a trip and cut hazard

products.name: Oregon CS1500 15-Amp Corded Self-Sharpening Chainsaw
products.description:
The Oregon CS1500 includes a PowerSharp self-sharpening system, which restores the chain edge in seconds with a built-in stone. That solves the most common complaint about electric saws: dull chains that make a good motor feel weak. A low-kickback chain adds a safety margin.

The tradeoff is that the PowerSharp chain and stone are consumables, so ongoing cost is higher than with a conventional chain. Against the SENIX and CRAFTSMAN corded saws it is more convenient but less cheap to run.

Use the sharpener often and keep the bar oiled. When the stone wears out, replace the chain and stone together per the manual.

products.name: CRAFTSMAN 16-Inch 12-Amp Corded Electric Chainsaw
products.description:
The CRAFTSMAN is a 16 inch corded saw with a 12 amp motor and a low-kickback bar and chain. It is the simplest and most affordable way to get an electric saw with a useful bar length.

The tradeoff is power. A 12 amp motor has less torque than the 15 amp saws here, so it bogs on green or wet wood near the bar's limit. Against the Oregon it gives up self-sharpening convenience.

Keep the chain sharp and the cord short. Oil the bar and unplug before adjusting the chain.
products.bestFor: Light yard pruning and occasional limbing near an outlet.
pros: 16 inch bar at a modest cost
cons: 12 amp motor bogs in wet wood

buyingCriteria.explanation: A corded saw like the SENIX, Oregon or CRAFTSMAN gives unlimited runtime for the price of a cord and an outlet, while cordless saws like the EGO and Greenworks give freedom with limited battery. For a yard within 100 feet of power, corded is cheaper and simpler. For storm cleanup away from the house, a battery saw or a spare pack is the only practical choice. A common mistake is buying cordless for a yard where an outlet is always nearby and then fighting a flat pack in the middle of a job. Another is buying corded and discovering that the longest run you need is 150 feet, which calls for a heavy extension cord that costs nearly as much as a spare battery. Walk the property and measure before you decide.

Bar length sets the largest log you can cut in one pass. A 16 inch bar handles most limbs, small firewood and storm cleanup, and an 18 inch bar like the SENIX gives a little more reach. Electric saws are not built for large felling work because a motor cannot sustain the load a big bar demands for long. The bar should also be at least two inches longer than the log you intend to cut, so a 16 inch bar comfortably handles a 12 inch round. If you find yourself cutting from both sides to get through a log, the saw is too small for the job and the habit is both slow and risky.

For cordless saws, voltage sets the torque ceiling and amp-hours set the run time. The EGO 56V 2.5Ah pack is rated at up to 130 cuts in a 4 by 4, while the Greenworks 40V comes with a 4Ah pack and the SEESII includes two. If you own other tools on a platform, spare packs save the most money. Cold weather matters too: lithium packs lose output near freezing, so a saw that cuts well in the garage can feel sluggish on a winter storm cleanup unless the battery is kept warm until the moment you use it. Never judge a pack by amp-hours alone, because a high-drain saw load heats a small pack quickly and may trigger thermal protection before the pack is truly empty.

Brushless motors in the EGO, Greenworks and SEESII run cooler and last longer than brushed motors. Corded saws are rated in amps: 12 amp on the CRAFTSMAN and 15 amp on the SENIX and Oregon. A 15 amp motor has more torque, but a household circuit limits it, so do not expect gas-saw performance. In practice a corded 15 amp saw performs like a small gas saw on seasoned limbs but lags on wet, green or knotted wood, where torque rather than chain speed decides the pace. Let the saw reach full speed before it touches the wood and let the chain do the work instead of leaning on the bar, because a stalled motor overheats long before it breaks.

A chain brake, a low-kickback chain and a dual-action switch matter more than power. The CRAFTSMAN and Oregon list low-kickback designs. Use eye and hand protection, keep both hands on the saw and never cut above shoulder height. Corded saws add a cord to manage, so always cut away from the cord. Check that the chain stops quickly when you release the trigger, because that electric brake behavior is a feature unique to electric saws that gas saws cannot match. Keep the work area clear of bystanders and pets, and plan the cut so that the saw will never be pinched or pulled toward your body if the log shifts.

A dull chain makes any electric saw feel weak. The Oregon's PowerSharp system makes sharpening quick, while other saws need a file or a trip to a sharpener. Check chain tension before every use and fill the bar oil reservoir, because running dry burns the chain and bar quickly. A useful field test is to cut a dry softwood log: a sharp chain throws thick chips and pulls itself into the wood, while a dull one produces fine dust and demands pressure. If you need to lean on the saw, stop and fix the chain before you blame the motor or battery.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cutting capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared bar length and motor or battery size together. The SENIX at 18 inches sets the length end of the range. Claims on newer brands were treated as claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power source
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared corded runtime with cordless freedom. Battery size and platform depth were credited. Cord handling was a drawback.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for chain brakes, low-kickback chains and dual-action switches. Saws with documented provisions scored higher. No credit was given for undocumented claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Maintenance
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered chain care, oiling and the effect of self-sharpening features. The Oregon scored well for convenience. Replacement part availability was a minor factor, and so was warranty length.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed what the kit includes, such as batteries and chargers. Dual-battery kits scored higher on usability. Scores reflect spec sheets and owner feedback patterns.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: The SENIX, Oregon and CRAFTSMAN give unlimited runtime and cost less. They are tethered by a cord, so use a short, heavy-gauge extension cord.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: The EGO, Greenworks and SEESII give freedom and quiet operation. Runtime is limited by the battery, so carry a spare for longer jobs.

howToChoose.note: Choose corded if you work near an outlet and cordless if you do not.

rows: Want a big pack in the box

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a 16 inch bar or longer, a motor with enough torque, either unlimited runtime or two batteries, and a sharp chain. Heavy firewood work tires batteries quickly.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The SENIX 18-Inch is the best for sustained bucking near an outlet. The SEESII 16-Inch with two batteries is the best cordless choice.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you cut often, where the EGO's brushless motor and platform or the Oregon's self-sharpening system save time. Also spend more for a second battery.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you only prune occasionally. The CRAFTSMAN corded saw is enough.

maintenance.why: Running dry burns the chain and bar quickly.
A loose chain can derail and a tight one wears the bar.
Dull chains slow cutting and strain the motor.
Full or empty storage shortens battery life.
A nicked cord is a shock and fire hazard.

faq.q: Can an electric chainsaw replace a gas saw?
faq.a: For limbing, small firewood and light felling, yes. For large trees or heavy daily use, a gas saw remains stronger. Electric suits occasional homeowners.
Corded gives unlimited runtime at a lower cost but ties you to an outlet. Cordless gives freedom but limited run time. Choose by where you cut.

faq.q: How many cuts does a battery give?
faq.a: Makers rate cuts in 4 by 4 lumber, such as up to 130 cuts for the EGO 2.5Ah. Real cuts depend on wood species and chain sharpness.

faq.q: What extension cord do I need?
faq.a: Use a short, heavy-gauge cord rated for the saw's amperage. A long thin cord causes voltage drop and overheating. Keep the cord behind you.
Yes. Low-kickback chains reduce but do not remove it. Use proper technique and keep both hands on the saw.

faq.q: How do I store the battery?
faq.a: Keep it indoors at partial charge, away from freezing temperatures. Cold reduces output and storage at full charge shortens life.
